According to the police report, a review of Motorworks's surveillance footage revealed that five to seven offenders stole many key fobs and began stealing luxury vehicles at six in the morning. They were in the middle of stealing their second round of cars when police arrived. 27-year-old Tavarius Jackson was charged with two counts of aggravated possession of a stolen vehicle, criminal damage to property, aggravated battery to a peace officer, and aggravated fleeing and eluding. A second suspect, 23-year-old Lamont Jackson was arrested two miles south of motorworks after crashing the second Mercedes that fled the lot. He was charged with aggravated fleeing and eluding and possession of a stolen motor vehicle. Both suspects were held on a $100,000 bond, and both suspects were on parole for prior felony convictions. According to the Illinois Department of Corrections, Tavarius received a four-year prison sentence for two counts of burglary and three counts of possessing a stolen vehicle. He was released April 2025 and is on parole through spring of 2026. Lamont received five years for burglary, aggravated reckless driving, and possession of a stolen vehicle, and is currently serving his time at Pinckneyville Correctional Center. According to the police report, The black Porsche was never located. In all, five people sustained injuries in four separate crashes caused by the group of thieves, and all involved have made a full recovery. Injus still once, they came back for seconds, same lives, same plan, and same arrogance. That's not a random crime, that's a system, and when you see it play out in broad daylight, it's hard not to wonder how deep this network really goes. When a crew walks into a car dealership during the daylight, they're sending a message, we're not hiding. And that kind of boldness doesn't just shock people, it shakes the foundation of what safety of the means. You can't script stuff like this because one-minute officers are responding to suspicious activity at a dealership. The next, the Porsche is ramming a squad car with the cops still inside. And that's not just a felony, it's a message, and that's I don't care about getting caught and I dare you to try and stop me. Timing is everything because early morning thefts means low patrol presence, lower dispatch response, and open highways for quick transport. Crews like this do not operate solo, the answer to a bitter boss, sometimes even interstate syndicists that move stolen luxury cars probably faster than banks move money. Now, federal prosecutors in the Eastern District of Missouri working with the Justice Department's Violent Crime and racketeering section recently indicted 10 members of an organized theft ring called the Strikers. This crew hit more than 20 dealerships across eastern Missouri and southern Illinois, stealing around 50 high-end cars. Hellcats, Trackhawks, BMWs, Audi's, Mercedes, worth $3 million. And they didn't just take the car as they stole kefob's plates and caused major property damage later flipping the stolen vehicles on social media for as little as $500 to $10,000. These thefts aren't isolated incidents. They're symptoms of a larger well-coordinated criminal economy stretching across state lines. I don't believe this was three random criminals. It was a test run from a machine bigger than them. Barrington was just a doubt on the map that morning, but make no mistake, someone higher up is counting the profits while police deal with the madness. Thank you.
